Artificial intelligence (AI) has played a role in life sciences research and healthcare delivery for decades, though its nature and applications have changed with each new technology. As early as the 1950s, symbolic logic models provided clinical decision support: a form of deterministic AI encoded human knowledge as rules that an AI logic model could follow and implement (Nawaz et al., 2025). These early rule-based systems highlighted both the promise and limitations of symbolic AI. Subsequent periods of over-expectation followed by underdelivery contributed to recurring "AI winters" in which investment and enthusiasm declined.After 2010, computational and algorithmic developments led to machine learning (ML) and deep learning models. While these performed extremely well in some use cases (Habehh and Gohel, 2021), notably in biomedical research and image analysis, their use remained largely concentrated among technical experts and specialized applications. In the 2020s, large language models (LLMs) have rapidly changed the AI landscape in life sciences and medicine, and we are on the cusp of even faster evolutions, with state space models and active inference-based concepts that could lead to non-linear, novel leaps.The adoption of LLMs has been unlike that of any other modern technology. Most innovations, such as cars, mobile phones, and the internet, have taken years (between 1 year and 75 years) to reach adoption by 50 million users globally (Desjardins, 2018), whereas ChatGPT took only 5 days to achieve this. This unprecedented uptake leads to a paradigm shift in how we think about the users, use cases, and impact of a new technology. LLMs could change working practices in nearly every industry, to varying degrees. In their lead article, Guni et al. articulate the potential influence of LLMs in life sciences research and healthcare delivery (Guni et al. 2026). They review the rise and fall of AI applications in biomedical research and clinical decision support, and robustly discuss the elements needed for the current wave of AI to succeed. Specifically, they comment that "multidisciplinary effort (is needed) across several key domains: i) algorithmic science and architectures, ii) datasets, iii) processing power and efficiency, iv) infrastructure, v) human factors through codesign, and vi) interoperability with both legacy and modern healthcare systems." These efforts will require collaboration between clinicians, researchers, technologists, patients, ethicists, policymakers and others, and Guni et al. discuss a thorough breadth and depth of key topics. However, a seventh critical domain underlies all the others: the transformation of biomedical education and workforce development. Without a workforce capable of effectively leading AI systems, even the most sophisticated algorithms, datasets, and infrastructure will fail to deliver lasting impact, and we risk another AI winter.With respect to education, the widespread yet heterogenous use of LLMs by students and professors alike is challenging current pedagogy and assessment frameworks. In some cases, students are using LLMs to study or complete homework assignments, yet their professors lack expertise and are unprepared to alter their syllabus, homework, or exams (Lelescu et al 2025). In other cases, faculty are trying to integrate LLMs but are being met by significant resistance by students (Farinosi and Melchior, 2025). LLMs are also changing the day-to-day activities of our workforce, where adoption is similarly mixed and there is limited infrastructure to support broad, comprehensive workforce development. Many proposed educational responses focus primarily on the development of AI competencies across the continuum of learners and professionals. However, an exclusive focus on AI competencies introduces two related risks: "cognitive de-skilling", in which professionals gradually lose critical expertise and skills due to over-reliance on AI and "never-skilling", where the next generation of learners never fully develops foundational competencies because AI systems perform those tasks from the outset.Currently, health systems plan to measure the immediate augmented performance of AI tools in terms of clinical outcomes or immediate workflow efficiencies; we have yet to comprehensively measure their impact on retained competency or the longer-term implications of their use as a performance standard. Over the next 50 years, AI will likely become a critical part of many decision-making processes, training programs, and assessments done in clinical settings. However, if we never measure the retained competency of clinical staff to understand the impact of AI on long-term skill erosion, we could unintentionally introduce a critical system failure in the future. Clinicians who can no longer spot errors in AI tools or perform tasks when tools fail may put patients at risk and create a new type of AI winter-a systemic failure due to over-reliance on AI and lack of human competency. This AI winter would be extremely damaging to the practice of medicine in multiple ways: 1) direct risk to patients, 2) time to re-skill a generation of medical practitioners, and 3) lack of medical leaders with expertise to train the clinicians.Life sciences and healthcare are not the first knowledge-intensive domains to confront the challenge of maintaining human expertise as automation becomes increasingly capable. As commercial aviation systems evolved to automate key functions such as takeoff, landing, and navigation, concerns emerged that pilots were becoming overly reliant on automation, potentially eroding critical manual flying skills and reducing resilience when automated systems failed. Recognizing this risk, the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a Safety Alert in 2017 (FAA, 2017) and further guidance in 2022 (FAA, 2022) to strengthen policies and training that preserved pilot proficiency in manual operations.This experience provides a compelling parallel to the adoption of AI-driven clinical decision support systems. In both aviation and healthcare, humans and technology function as components of a sociotechnical system (Trist, 1981), where safety depends on the effective interaction between people, processes, and tools. When technological capabilities advance without corresponding attention to human competencies, organizations risk losing the very redundancies that protect against failure. The FAA's approach demonstrates that successful integration of automation requires more than technical performance; it requires deliberate governance, training, monitoring, and ongoing investment in human expertise. Ultimately, the safety of any automated system depends not only on the technology itself, but also on how human competency is preserved and strengthened alongside it (Macnamara et al., 2024).In short, humans must be the redundancy when technology systems fail.To avoid creating a generation of professionals who cannot function effectively when AI systems are unavailable, unreliable, or incorrect, we need radical transformation in our education and workforce development frameworks to teach both AI competencies and domain-specific competencies in synchrony. We must develop these competency frameworks now to prepare the future workforce to thrive in an AI-enabled world.Perhaps the easier competency framework is that of AI competencies. For example, prompt engineering, AI literacy, validation and oversight, ethical and responsible use of AI, agentic AI, and the nature of human-AI collaborations are obvious topics that biomedical education for life sciences research and healthcare delivery must begin to learn. Many programs around the globe have begun offering didactic and practical-based educational programs to serve this need. Perhaps more challenging is the listing of domain-specific competencies. Not every fact that previous generations were expected to memorize will remain equally valuable in an AI-enabled environment. The challenge lies in determining which foundational knowledge remains essential for independent critical thinking and reasoning, and which tasks can appropriately be augmented by AI. Future domain-specific competency frameworks may place less emphasis on memorization and greater emphasis on reasoning, interpretation, critical evaluation, communication, judgement, and collaboration. Each domain needs to develop their list of domain-specific competencies and then design pedagogy, training, and learning assessment around these competencies, assuming that AI will be a partner for the learner. Neither AI competencies nor domain-specific competencies alone are sufficient; future professionals will require mastery of both.The goal should be to leverage AI to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of biomedical research and clinical practice, allowing humans to focus on uniquely human activities such as critical thinking, creativity, and interpersonal connection, rather than repetitive and mundane tasks.Our society has seen workforce transitions before, for example as result of the invention of electricity, the Industrial Revolution, and the emergence of the internet. For example, online streaming services have rendered many jobs unnecessary, such as cashiers in video rental or record stores, while creating thousands of jobs never imagined in the 1990s. Similarly, if the current AI era succeeds some workforce roles will vanish, but many new roles will emerge, some unimaginable today. Leaders, researchers, educators, and workforce members must proactively develop systems and frameworks that enable current and future generations to thrive with AI technology at their fingertips.The future of biomedical research and healthcare should not be defined by "humans in the loop", but by "humans in the lead". Our challenge is not simply to build more capable AI systems. It is to build educational and workforce development frameworks that preserve human expertise while enabling effective human-AI partnership, i.e., systems that are "human-led, AI-enabled." History suggests that AI winters occur when technological capabilities outpace the ability of institutions, professionals, and society to effectively adopt and sustain them. Workforce transformation may therefore be one of the most important safeguards against another cycle of overpromising and underdelivering. If we succeed, AI can become one of the most transformative technologies in the history of medicine. If we fail, another AI winter may be closer than we think.

documents.abstract: This quasi-experimental study investigated the differential effects of human teacher feedback (HTF), AI-generated feedback (AIGF), and hybrid feedback (HF) on learner engagement and argumentative writing quality among 120 undergraduate ESL students across an eight-week intervention. Engagement (behavioural, cognitive, emotional) was measured via a purpose-built questionnaire and revision-tracking logs; writing quality was scored on a five-dimension analytic rubric. Repeated-measures ANOVA and multiple regression showed that HF was associated with the greatest improvement in writing quality (η²p = .24), HTF with the highest proportion of higher-order revisions, and AIGF with the highest revision frequency. Hybrid feedback condition membership was the strongest predictor of writing-quality improvement, followed by cognitive engagement. These findings have implications for AI-integrated writing instruction in higher education.

documents.abstract: This conference presentation examines the multifaceted impact of artificial intelligence (AI) proliferation on internet security, cybersecurity practices, software engineering, and digital sovereignty. It considers both the defensive capabilities enabled by AI technologies and the emerging security risks associated with their widespread adoption. The presentation discusses how AI-based solutions can improve cyberattack detection, threat analysis, incident response, and vulnerability identification. At the same time, it highlights the growing potential for malicious applications, including automated malware generation, phishing, deepfakes, social engineering, and disinformation. Particular attention is devoted to security vulnerabilities in AI-driven and agentic systems, including prompt injection, jailbreaking, training data poisoning, goal hijacking, and context manipulation. The analysis addresses the risks associated with excessive system privileges, persistent access to external tools, non-deterministic behavior, and dependencies on untrusted information sources. Security mitigation approaches include static and dynamic application security testing, the principle of least privilege, zero-trust architectures, sandboxed execution, and input/output validation. The presentation also explores the implications of AI-assisted software development, emphasizing the necessity of comprehensive code review, testing, and validation. It identifies potential challenges associated with vibe coding, cognitive debt, declining opportunities for junior developers, and the erosion of organizational knowledge and technical expertise. Broader societal and regulatory considerations include digital sovereignty, technological dependencies, open-source alternatives, responsible AI governance, and emerging European initiatives supporting technological autonomy. The presentation concludes that artificial intelligence can become a strategic asset for cybersecurity when AI models are developed using high-quality data, deployed within appropriate security frameworks, and subjected to effective human oversight and governance.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within Italian educational contexts represents one of the most complex digital transitions of the contemporary world (Han et al., 2022; Hopcan et al., 2023). Following the pandemic experience and the lockdown, schools have witnessed a proliferation of training offers for teachers, both curricular and specialized in support, often characterized by huge efforts. In this scenario, AI cannot be reduced to a simple instrumental innovation; in fact, it requires a profound redefinition of educational design and professional roles. Abandoning an initial technooptimism, international research today requires a critical-reflective approach: integrating these technologies without analyzing their ethical assumptions risks amplifying existing inequalities. As a result, the distinction proposed in the literature between an AI used "instead of education", which replaces the relationship, and an AI used "for education", which acts in support of human pedagogical goals, becomes fundamental (Holmes et al., 2022). documents.abstract: ABSTRACT: This study investigated the influence of artificial intelligence and learning analytics on the performance of postgraduate students in universities in Cross River State, Nigeria. The study specifically examined the influence of artificial intelligence technologies, ethical implications of artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and ethical implications of learning analytics on postgraduate students’ learning. Four research questions and four null hypotheses guided the study. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. The study was conducted in public universities offering postgraduate programmes in Cross River State. A sample of 300 postgraduate students was selected using a multistage sampling technique involving purposive, stratified random, and proportionate sampling procedures. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled *Artificial Intelligence and Learning Analytics Influence Questionnaire (AILAIQ)*. The instrument was validated by three experts in Educational Technology and Measurement and Evaluation, while a reliability coefficient of 0.84 was obtained using Cronbach’s Alpha. Data collected were analyzed using simple linear regression to answer the research questions, while regression t-test was used to test the null hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that artificial intelligence technologies had a significant positive influence on postgraduate students’ learning, accounting for 6.7% of the variance in learning outcomes (R = .259, R² = .067, t = 5.132, p < .05). Ethical implications of artificial intelligence also had a significant influence, accounting for 13.3% of the variance (R = .365, R² = .133, t = 7.512, p < .05). Learning analytics significantly influenced postgraduate students’ learning, although its contribution was relatively small, accounting for 1.2% of the variance (R = .109, R² = .012, t = 2.107, p = .036). Similarly, ethical implications of learning analytics significantly influenced postgraduate students’ learning, accounting for 7.9% of the variance (R = .282, R² = .079, t = 5.627, p < .05). Based on these findings, the study concluded that artificial intelligence and learning analytics, as well as the ethical conditions surrounding their use, significantly influence postgraduate students’ learning in universities in Cross River State. The study recommended, among others, that universities should strategically integrate AI and learning analytics into postgraduate education, develop clear ethical frameworks for their use, strengthen digital infrastructure, and provide adequate training for lecturers and students on the responsible and effective use of these technologies. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, learning analytics, ethical implications, postgraduate students, academic performance, universities, Cross River State.

In the age of the Fourth Revolution, understood not only as the convergence of cyber -physical systems and artificial intelligence but also as a mutation of human self-understanding, the sharp distinction between online and offline dissolves into a constitutively hybrid "onlife" condition. Digital environments do not merely transmit information: they orchestrate emotional states, modulate attention and construct reputational identities, acting upon a subjectivity solicited from within rather than repressed from without. Setting out from Asimov's short story Evidence and the figure of the "maimed master", the essay locates the true terrain of the educational challenge not in computational power but in empathy and affectivity. The risk is not that machines will become human, but that humanity will grow accustomed to a synthetic affectivity, devoid of the weight of the body and of the responsibility inherent in relationship. In many work environments, professionals perform physically demanding routines involving repetitive movements and prolonged static postures, increasing exposure to biomechanical risk factors associated with work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs). Wearable technologies offer opportunities for continuous posture monitoring and real-time feedback, but their occupational deployment remains challenging due to limitations related to comfort, durability, energy autonomy, and integration with work clothing. This scoping review aims to synthesize and critically analyze the existing evidence on smart-textile-based wearable systems for occupational posture monitoring. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, a systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and CINAHL was conducted, identifying 566 records. After screening and eligibility assessment, 34 studies were included in the final synthesis. The included studies were analyzed according to wearable architectures, sensing technologies, data processing and posture recognition, user feedback mechanisms, and energy management strategies. Hybrid architectures combining textile-based sensors and inertial measurement units, together with machine learning and real-time feedback, emerged as promising approaches for continuous posture monitoring. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical or laboratory validation, with relatively small samples and limited long-term evaluation in real occupational environments. Five studies reported changes in posture or ergonomic behavior following the use of the technology, while no direct evidence of reductions in WRMSD incidence or severity was identified. Overall, the findings demonstrate substantial technological potential for smart-textile-based posture monitoring, but current evidence is insufficient to establish clinical or occupational effectiveness in preventing WRMSDs. Future research should prioritize prospective, long-term validation involving larger and more diverse worker populations under real-world occupational conditions, while addressing comfort, durability, energy autonomy, and compatibility with occupational clothing and personal protective equipment.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence within educational environments is profoundly reshaping language teaching. Language teachers are increasingly expected to operate in digitally mediated environments and to integrate technological tools into their pedagogical practice (Godwin-Jones, 2022). Yet resistance remains widespread. Without adequate training that addresses both the technical and pedagogical dimensions of AI use, hesitation is a predictable and, in many respects, rational response. The literature confirms that resistance to AI adoption stems from a structural deficit: limited preparation, insufficient theoretical grounding, and the absence of models that connect technological tools to principled language pedagogy (Godwin-Jones, 2022; Kovačić & Bubaš, 2023). This challenge is particularly acute in LSP education, where language learning is inseparable from disciplinary discourse, professional communication, and context-sensitive language use. Specialized discourse cannot be reduced to automated linguistic processing, and teachers who lack a robust pedagogical framework struggle to evaluate what AI tools can and cannot do within their specific instructional contexts. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 349-350. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Abstract Rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities worldwide to issue guidelines on student AI use in assessment. While existing research catalogues policy content and student misuse, little is known about how students perceive these guidelines and how such perceptions shape behaviour. This paper argues that current research treats guidelines as a binary intervention—present or absent—overlooking their psychological and institutional authenticity. Drawing on procedural justice and neutralisation theories, we contend that when guidelines are vague, invisible, unenforceable, and treated by academics as box-ticking exercises, they fail as integrity safeguards and may instead provide justifications for disingenuous AI use. We further argue that this pattern reflects institutional compulsions—legal, reputational, and competitive—that drive guideline issuance despite known limitations. We propose a research agenda centred on guideline authenticity and its effects on fairness perceptions, moral neutralisation, and compliance intentions, alongside perceptions of institutional motivation. A sequential mixed-methods design is outlined, drawing on UAE and UK contexts. The agenda aims to move institutional practice beyond symbolic policy-making toward genuinely embedded academic integrity cultures.

The growing use of artificial intelligence in education raises questions about how emotional experience, relational care, and professional responsibility can be sustained in increasingly data-mediated teaching environments. This conceptual article examines instructional emotion as an interrelated configuration of teachers’ emotional engagement, students’ learning-related experiences, and the affective relationships through which teaching acquires meaning. Drawing on scholarship on achievement emotions, caring pedagogy, teacher–student relationships, and artificial intelligence in education, the article organizes its analysis around three value foundations: embodied human experience, relational connection, and teachers’ professional responsibility. It then identifies four potential forms of alienation arising when technological efficiency overrides educational judgment: procedural rigidity in teaching methods, emotional distance in interaction, the loss of affective meaning in content, and the reduction of assessment to measurable performance. Corresponding reconstruction pathways include emotionally adaptive instructional design, humanistic interaction, affective knowledge graphs, and emotionally responsive assessment. These pathways are guided by teacher judgment and bounded by consent, fairness, transparency, and human oversight. The framework distinguishes the interpretation of emotional evidence from claims to measure learners’ inner states directly. Its contribution is to connect educational values, potential risks, and pedagogical responses within a coherent conceptual structure. The proposed relationships remain open to empirical examination across educational settings.

Oman’s digitisation priorities under Oman Vision 2040 encourage the integration of technology into teaching and learning. Little research examines instructors’ perceptions of Microsoft Teams (MS Teams) Reading Progress in Omani General Foundation Programme (GFP) contexts, particularly regarding its pedagogical value, ease of use, and implementation challenges. This mixed-methods pilot study explored instructors’ perceptions of Reading Progress in General English 2 (GE2), within the pre-degree GFP at the Preparatory Studies Centre (PSC), University of Technology and Applied Sciences (UTAS), Oman. MS Teams Reading Progress is an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported tool designed to help students practice reading aloud, improve accuracy and fluency, and give instructors performance data. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), this study explored instructors’ perceptions of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, social influence, facilitating conditions, and behavioural intention. Using purposive sampling, data were collected from three sources: a structured questionnaire (N = 10), two semi-structured interviews, and MS Teams usage logs. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and qualitative data were analysed thematically. The findings reveal a disconnect between teachers’ positive perceptions and willingness to continue using the tool and students’ limited engagement. Although instructors believed the tool could support reading fluency and accuracy, its use remained low, possibly due to the timing of the pilot, the absence of continuous assessment (CA), and limited time within the course plan. The findings indicate that wider implementation would benefit from early rollout, integration into course design, and CA weighting.

This white paper is the deliverable of work package 2.5 “Interdisciplinary evaluation protocols” (german: “Interdisziplinäre Evaluierungsprotokolle”) of the Center for Assistive Technologies Rhein-Ruhr (Zentrum Assistive Technologien Rhein-Ruhr, ZAT, see Wild-Wall et al. 2024). It addresses the evaluation of assistive technology (AT), which we define as any device, software, equipment, or system that enables people with disabilities, functional limitations or special needs to perform specific tasks. The purpose of evaluating AT is to assess, in a systematic and reproducible manner, how effectively it fulfills its intended function in close interplay with the human user(s). Because AT, by definition, interacts with people, its evaluation must account not only for technological performance but also for social and human factors. A meaningful and comprehensive evaluation therefore requires an interdisciplinary perspective, drawing on the methodological toolkits of multiple disciplines and approaches.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the university landscape offers unprecedented efficiency and speed, radically transforming how students access information and fulfill their academic responsibilities. However, this instantaneous convenience gives rise to a critical shift: do contemporary students remain autonomous knowledge producers, or have they been reduced to mere curators who synthesize and rearrange content from digital repositories? This paper critically examines the dynamics of student learning and assignment completion amidst the expanding AI ecosystem. Employing a reflective-critical approach, the article highlights the paradox of digital efficiency—which accelerates academic processes on one hand, yet risks diminishing critical depth, intellectual autonomy, and student creativity on the other. The analysis reveals that the relationship between students and AI is not merely instrumental; rather, it actively reshapes structural study habits, demanding a profound pedagogical redefinition to ensure that university institutions preserve the fundamental essence of knowledge creation.

documents.abstract: At the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly this year, more than 150 official statements on data, digital health, and artificial intelligence (AI) were delivered by 74 countries and 10 regional blocs, alongside 42 side events, and over 30 Ministers of Health affirming digital transformation as a core feature of resilient health systems. The through line was consistent across every region: countries are calling for concerted global leadership towards shared standards and clear governance to validate, benchmark, and regulate AI in health.Sustainable, effective AI requires an ecosystem to function, and often carries real risks to data sovereignty, privacy, and equity. AI trained on incomplete data, tested in narrow settings, or deployed without attention to bias and local context can reproduce, and even amplify, the very inequities it aims to close. It is against this backdrop that we read the lead article by Guni et al. on "large language medicine (1)." We share the authors' optimism but sharpen their central question: not whether generative and multimodal AI will reshape medicine, but how we build the scaffolding that ensures the reshaping happens safely, equitably, and sustainably.Deep learning, generative AI, large language models (LLMs), and connected agentic systems promise both incremental and transformative change across diagnostics, disease management, surveillance, prevention, and drug discovery. Yet, as Guni et al. candidly note, today's clinically mature, regulator-approved tools remain predominantly diagnostic and built on older machine learning architectures. LLMs have not yet crossed into routine practice; interconnected agentic systems are being introduced only in a fraction of cutting-edge facilities. Health systems and clinical medicine, although a rich proving ground for technical experimentation and innovation, are also understandably cautious and risk averse. The principles of evidence-based medicine further solidify the need for requisite, repeated, and rigorous demonstration of efficacy before well-established practices are altered. Some Author 1 et al. Short title/running header 4 critique this caution as innovation recalcitrance; given the duty of care in health, it is better understood as the scientific scrutiny that any clinical tool, however heavily promoted, should be expected to survive.An AI solution does not scale on its own; it scales when an ecosystem for scale exists or is built around it. This includes clear regulatory capacity and governance, strong health information systems, and trained health personnel. We posit that a key element of that enabling foundation is digital public infrastructure for health. Some of the most durable gains come not from what makes headlines but from the unglamorous parts of the system no one photographs: the unique identifiers and information exchanges, the semantic standards which allow systems to interoperate, powering supply chains that keep essential medicines on the shelf, and persistent records that follow a patient across facilities within a health system to maintain continuity of care. Countries that adopted monolithic, donor-funded digital health tools have already seen those systems collapse when funding shifted; language models deployed as parallel silos, disconnected from a shared reference architecture, risk repeating that failure at greater speed and scale. Technology-neutral reference architectures, developed collaboratively across health and telecommunications agencies and built on open standards, offer a map for where these foundations should sit (2). AI cannot pervade "every aspect of medicine," as Guni et al. envision, without an underlying layer of high-quality data structured for interoperability, disciplined evaluation protocols, and the systems analysis required to introduce AI into existing clinical workflows. Experimental systems may be introduced into clinical practice, but without clear proof points and performance benchmarks, their transition from pilot to clinical standard will likely be slow and inequitable. Ministries and hospital systems are already experiencing a glut of vendors promising impressive solutions to long-standing challenges, often without the accompanying (3,4), or countries with the least regulatory capacity will simply import externally reviewed systems without local ownership. Regulatory sandboxes, such as the United Kingdom's AI Airlock, which allows supervised testing of AI tools that fit no existing device category (5), remain an underused bridge between principle and practice. Harmonization does not mean uniformity; it means enough common evidentiary ground that a safety finding in one country still holds in another, since the models themselves will cross borders faster than any single regulator's jurisdiction can follow. Language, disease burden, health system maturity, and data availability vary enormously; a model validated in one setting cannot be assumed safe in another. Multi-institutional, privacy-preserving evaluation designed into deployment from the start, not bolted on afterward, should be the norm, particularly for populations already under-represented in training data. This brings us to what authentic inclusion in AI design actually looks like. It is not access to a shared global model. It is each country's ability to shape a model on the data of its own population, keep it under its own governance, regulate it according to its own values and context, and operate it through a health workforce with the capacity to evaluate its outputs. A ministry that cannot inspect a model, audit its performance against its own population's outcomes, or withdraw it from clinical use does not exercise meaningful oversight.Sovereignty in this context is not isolation; it is knowing where data sit, who processes them, under whose law, and on what terms access can be revoked. Without populationrepresentative data, locally grounded regulation, and a trained workforce able to question and override the system where necessary, the populations furthest behind will bear the greatest exposure to model failure, precisely because they are least represented in training data and least resourced to identify when a system is underperforming. This is a critical moment to set a shared direction for how AI in health is governed. Background: Fresh graduates face an increasingly difficult school-to-work transition, while artificial intelligence (AI) has become a routine study and job-search companion; yet how the intention to use AI translates into employability, and through which mechanisms, remains unclear. Objective: Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study tests whether behavioral intention to use AI is associated with self-perceived graduate employability directly and indirectly through career adaptability and job search self-efficacy, and whether AI self-efficacy and AI trust moderate these paths. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey of 612 Indonesian fresh graduates who use AI for career preparation was analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: AI use intention positively predicted career adaptability (β = 0.305) and job search self-efficacy (β = 0.249), and both resources predicted self-perceived employability. The indirect paths through both resources were significant, and a direct effect of AI use intention on employability remained, indicating partial mediation. AI self-efficacy and AI trust showed significant main effects on their resources, while the interaction-related indirect effects were not significant. Conclusion: AI use intention is associated with self-perceived employability through career adaptability and job search self-efficacy. The cross-sectional findings do not establish causality. Educational institutions and career-service units may use these findings to inform structured AI-supported occupational exploration, skills-gap analysis, résumé refinement, and interview rehearsal, while encouraging critical verification of AI outputs.

Abstract As AI agents start to act in European critical infrastructure (telecom networks, payment systems, cloud platforms and industrial robots), a recurring gap appears. A system can log that an operation was authorized and acknowledged, yet still be unable to show that the evidence behind it was current, or that the reported result matches what actually happened. This gap matters to obligations under the EU AI Act, including: risk management (Article 9); record-keeping and logging (Article 12); human oversight (Article 14); accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15); post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting (Articles 72–73). This publication presents the foundational part of a 15-part technical series, also submitted as an IETF Internet-Draft. It defines a vendor-neutral evidence-consistency framework built on these elements: every consequential operation receives a stable identity and a declared verification objective; each observation carries its provenance, resource generation, time interval and clock uncertainty; domain-specific checks produce a scoped three-valued result: SUPPORTED, CONTRADICTED or UNRESOLVED. UNRESOLVED is a first-class outcome. Missing or stale evidence is recorded honestly rather than reported as success, which gives auditors, oversight personnel and incident investigators a reconstructable decision record. The framework keeps verification separate from authority. A positive result never grants permission to act; any consequential effect stays under a separate, accountable control boundary. Acknowledgement, completion, physical outcome and financial settlement are reconciled as independent evidence. A three-layer architecture keeps shared evidence semantics apart from twelve domain profiles: radio access and network incident recovery; telecom sessions and charging; hardware and DMA command paths; multi-agent negotiation and asynchronous tools; robotics and physical safety; multilingual emergency instructions; browser agents and agent migration; autonomous commerce; accelerator reset. The material is also relevant to engineering work under NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act, DORA and the Machinery Regulation. The PDF includes: a reader's summary with diagrams; an analytical latency and capacity model with a measurement plan; 12 proposed verification tests; threat and edge-case profiles; a searchable catalogue of 639 engineering mechanisms. The document describes technical mechanisms and makes no legal-compliance, certification or conformity claim.

documents.abstract: This exploration examines the impact of supplementary AI-generated explanatory materials on foundational mathematics learning and creative metacognition in primary education. The study followed a quantitative, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design with a nonequivalent control group. Fourth-grade classes in five schools were assigned to conditions at the classroom level: an intervention group receiving AI-facilitated handouts (n = 135) and a control group using programmatic textbooks (n = 128). Students in the experimental condition received eight supplementary lessons featuring paper-based handouts. These handouts presented explanations, examples, and illustrations of new mathematical topics generated by a large language model (Gemini 2.5 Pro), prompted the inclusion of age-appropriate content and a dedicated section encouraging creative metacognition (reflection and novel idea generation). Baseline equivalence was confirmed. The outcomes assessed included single-digit mental arithmetic, multidigit calculation, arithmetic word problem-solving, and creative metacognition, which were analyzed via multilevel or robust linear modeling accounting for classroom clustering. The results indicated no statistically significant differences between groups on single-digit mental arithmetic tasks. However, students who received AI-generated materials showed significantly greater improvement in multidigit calculation tasks and one-step word problem-solving than did the control group. No significant difference was found for multistep word problems. The intervention group also presented a substantially greater increase in creative metacognition scores than did the control group. The findings provide preliminary quasi-experimental evidence that curated, static AI-generated explanations, when designed to include metacognitive prompts, may be associated with greater gains in specific procedural and applied mathematical skills and creative metacognition among fourth-grade students under the conditions studied. This approach illustrates how generative AI can be leveraged as an authoring tool to supplement standard instruction and cultivate higher-order cognitive skills in young learners.

Evaluation of medical AI has inherited its instruments from the evaluation of people: examinations, expert judgement of free text, and task value denominated in the hours a practitioner would need. This working paper asks which of those instruments survive when the thing measured is a silicon producer (a model running inside a harness with tools) and builds a measurement framework for the parts that do not. It is the argument for the construction of the MedGauge Methodology, version 0.1.0 (https://medgauge.org/methodology/text/), which is the normative text. It tests the claim that silicon producers differ from human producers against the literature and finds twelve properties of silicon producers that bear on measurement, each stated with its counter-evidence; a difference from people is supported for two of them by an opened source, three hold by construction of the subject, and for the remaining seven no source states the human side and no difference is asserted. It shows that human-anchored evaluations divide into anchors on human time (which transfer as a predictor of difficulty but not as a unit), on a human product or rule (which transfer once the product is converted into a key of field checks set independently by two experts) and on human judgement of free text or preference (which do not transfer). On that basis it builds the measurement: following the international vocabulary of metrology, the reference of each quantity moves from a unit to a versioned grading program applied to a fixed artifact contract. It gives scale rules for labels, levels and counts; proposes base and derived quantities with their scale type, traceability and cross-harness comparability; maps them onto ten measurement dimensions and ten task labels; and sets out an examination regime in which a subject passes only if every task passes in all three runs with no safety veto, the strength of a pass being a one-sided 95% lower bound on reliability, with execution errors counted as failures, paired comparison with step-down multiplicity control, and no overall score. Version 0.1.0 of the methodology sets no level threshold and issues no level. The paper proposes a four-layer task typology with its literature base, explains why a closed, uncalibrated, generated task set licenses an attribute-sampling regime but not a response-model regime, and sets out the uncertainty budget for the chain from a published score to its public source clause. Standardised semantics for products, scenarios and task types, and the validation of those standards, are set out as a research plan, not as results. The paper reports no measurement result. At the date of publication the public site is live, no benchmark round has been run, no result record exists and every leaderboard is empty.

documents.abstract: In 2024, revision of the Enforcement Decree of the Higher Education Act in Korea abolished the rigid division between the 2-year premedical phase and the 4-year medical phase, allowing medical schools to design 6-year curricula autonomously for the first time in a century. Universities nationwide have begun redesigning their programs accordingly. This historic reform coincides with the rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence (AI) across society, including the ways students learn. In the current curriculum reform discourse, however, AI is discussed almost exclusively as content to be taught or as a supplementary tool to be used, whereas the more fundamental question of AI as an educational agent remains largely unexamined. Outside the formal curriculum, AI tutors already function as de facto teachers: a randomized experiment suggests that well-designed AI tutoring can outperform expert- led active-learning classrooms, and international surveys indicate that medical students routinely consult AI before, or instead of, their professors. This paper argues that the widening gap between the official, faculty-centered curriculum and the actual AI-mediated learning ecosystem may create discord: AI-mediated learning may become an unmanaged informal curriculum, faculty-designed assessment may lose authority, and trust in the formal curriculum may erode. Curriculum reform that merely rearranges the 6-year structure without addressing who teaches risks producing an elaborate design for an education that no longer reflects how learning occurs. Medical schools should explicitly define the position, scope, and governance of AI as an educational agent within their new curricula.

This study examines the theological significance of the doctrine of Imago Dei in response to the ethical challenges posed by artificial intelligence to human dignity and identity. Utilizing a qualitative literature review approach, the research analyzes how technological advancements in AI necessitate a profound reflection on theological anthropology. The findings indicate that the Imago Dei remains the foundational framework for affirming human uniqueness and dignity amidst digital progress. Consequently, AI development and utilization must be guided by Christian ethical principles to ensure technology supports human well-being without eroding core values. Ultimately, the study highlights the need for a contextual reconstruction of Christian spirituality and ethics, enabling believers to engage with AI wisely, responsibly, and in alignment with their divine calling as God's image.

documents.abstract: This contribution analyses the relationship between mirror neurons, Artificial Intelligence, Affective Computing, and educational technologies for the socio-emotional inclusion of students with ASD. Social robots, augmented reality, and intelligent systems are understood as pedagogical mediators, capable of making social cues more accessible and fostering personalised learning environments. The mirror neuron system offers a key framework for understanding the embodied nature of intersubjectivity. The sharing of neural codes between observed and executed actions allows imitation, empathy, and the understanding of others to be interpreted as processes integrating perception, action, and emotion (Gallese, 2008). Learning is thus a relational, situated experience. This framework dialogues with AI architectures. Artificial neural networks learn from data and generalise responses, but their pedagogical value depends on supporting adaptive interactions. Social robots, immersive environments, and augmented reality may offer structured contexts in which students exercise communicative and socio-emotional skills through feedback and recognisable routines. Introduction Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers significant opportunities to improve healthcare quality, especially in critical care settings, where timely decisions are essential yet challenging due to the volume of continuously accumulating patient data. AI algorithms can analyze data in real time, summarize key information for busy care teams, and alert clinicians to critical events and important care milestones. However, successful implementation requires first understanding the needs and barriers care teams face, including needs that are currently missing from their workflow, and what obstacles to integration exist. Methods To address these questions, we conducted a field study in a Cardiothoracic Intensive Care Unit (CT-ICU) to evaluate user needs for implementing real-time AI predictive analytics. We observed and interviewed fourteen participants ( n = 14), including nursing staff, advanced practice providers (NP/PAs), cardiovascular critical care attending physicians, and surgeons. Through a qualitative thematic analysis, we identified key considerations for developing and implementing static and real-time AI and predictive tools in the CT-ICU, aligning with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) constructs of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use . Findings Key themes included: (1) the system must have added clinical value to the clinical team and patients, (2) trust in the AI system should be prioritized through co-design processes, transparency in the system, and consistent prediction accuracy, and (3) integration into workflow was critical, including robust onboarding and minimizing alarm fatigue, charting burden, click burden, and technology burden with consideration of personal wellness. Conclusion As a synthesis of our findings, we identify a series of key design insights and suggest a preliminary framework for AI technology development focused on clinical team trust and adoption, the Trusted AI for Clinical Teams (TACT) framework. These findings offer the potential to bridge from AI research to clinical implementation.

documents.abstract: Aims Healthcare workers (HCWs) are frequently exposed to psychosocial job demands (JDs) that may lead to work-related stress. This study investigates the association between JDs—specifically time pressure, problem solving, overload, and emotional demands—and hair cortisol concentration (HCC), as biomarker of long-term hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis activation, in a sample of HCWs. It further examines the moderating role of negative affectivity (NA), an individual characteristic linked to heightened stress reactivity. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources theory and the allostatic load model, we hypothesized that (1) JDs would be positively associated with HCC and (2) this relationship would be stronger for individuals high in NA. Design Participants were 67 healthcare professionals working in a healthcare facility located in Northern Italy. Participants completed a self-report questionnaire designed to assess JDs and NA. Next, participants provided a hair sample for the assessment of HCC. Results Although data from a sample of HCWs revealed some positive but non-significant trends for problem solving and overload, generally JDs were not associated with HCC at average levels of NA. Interestingly, NA moderated the relationship between problem solving/time pressure and HCC, with stronger positive associations among individuals with high NA. Conclusion Findings from this exploratory cross-sectional study suggest that NA may act as a vulnerability factor, implying that HCWs high in NA may have a heightened strain response to certain JDs. By integrating psychological and biological measures, this study offers novel insights into the interplay between workplace stressors, personality traits, and physiological responses to stress. These findings highlight the potential relevance of individual differences in occupational stress research, and point to HCC as a promising indicator of chronic stress among HCWs. Implications for the profession The findings suggest the need for occupational health interventions tailored to individual traits, such as NA, to reduce stress reactivity, foster well-being, and enhance the quality of care provided.

Artificial intelligence tools — large language model chatbots, symptom checkers, AI-based interpretation of wearable-device data, and AI-generated or AI-translated medical content — are increasingly used by patients and families to obtain health information, which they then bring into clinical encounters. This shifts part of nurses' work from providing health information toward identifying, appraising, and calibrating patient-acquired information, including correcting misinformation, addressing questions rooted in AI-generated advice, and negotiating situations where AI-derived information conflicts with professional care recommendations. Two parallel strands exist in the nursing literature: (a) internet-era research on "internet-informed patients" and nurses' responses (L___), and (b) research on nurse–clinical-AI interaction (L___). The intersection — patients' use of AI for health information and nurses' responses — has not been systematically mapped: concept boundaries are unclear, evidence is scattered, and much of it is descriptive or anecdotal. This scoping review aims to map the extent, range, and nature of evidence at this intersection, clarify concepts, describe how nurse responses are studied and measured, and identify evidence gaps to inform practice guidance, health-education strategies, and future primary research. AI-specific evidence is at an early stage; a limited number of eligible Tier 1 sources is anticipated, and a nascent-evidence finding will be reported candidly rather than compensated for by post hoc broadening of eligibility. documents.abstract: The spread of digital technologies and artificial intelligence is profoundly transforming educational processes, necessitating a shift away from an exclusively technocentric view of innovation. As Selwyn (2016) and Floridi (2014) highlight, technologies are not mere tools, but environments that influence the construction of knowledge, relationships, and professional identities. The literature highlights how emotions, trust, and a sense of belonging significantly influence participation in digital environments ( Zembylas ,2015). From this perspective, social presence (Garrison, Anderson, & Archer, 2000) and psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999) become important. This paper analyses the role of an open digital space in building an emotionally aware learning environment within the specialisation courses for support activities (TFA). The research adopts a qualitative action research approach supported by descriptive quantitative data. The study involved 1,500 students enrolled in TFA programs from different Italian regions. This contribution presents an exploratory study on pre-service teachers' perceptions of the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in lesson planning, with a focus on opportunities, risks, and conditions for effective integration into instructional design. The study is grounded in the TPACK framework (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) and its extension Intelligent-TPACK (Celik, 2023), which incorporates an explicit ethical dimension into teachers' technological and pedagogical knowledge. Within this perspective, AI tools such as chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, and automated planning systems are not neutral instruments but sociotechnical systems that require critical evaluation in terms of transparency, fairness, and accountability. The theoretical approach adopted here is further informed by critical AI literacy perspectives, which emphasise the need for teachers to develop not only operational competence but also the ability to interrogate the assumptions and biases embedded in algorithmic outputs. The rapid adoption of generative AI (GenAI) among university students has raised concerns that excessive trust in AI outputs may erode critical thinking. This study examines how overtrust relates to critical thinking through cognitive offloading and AI dependency, with AI literacy as a protective moderator, integrating partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with machine learning. Survey data from 580 Vietnamese undergraduates were analysed through a five-step pipeline: exploratory structure learning, confirmatory path estimation, predictive benchmarking, explainable AI, and heterogeneous-effect estimation. Overtrust was associated with higher offloading (β = 0.390) and dependency (β = 0.402), both of which were associated with lower critical thinking (β = -0.251 and -0.348), while AI literacy buffered the association with dependency (interaction β = 0.154). Crucially, the direct effect of overtrust was non-significant and the two mediators carried 89% of its total effect, indicating indirect-only mediation. A parsimonious six-variable classifier separated at-risk students with AUC ≈ 0.77, whereas demographics alone performed at chance; SHAP analysis identified AI dependency as the dominant feature in the classification decision, and a causal forest confirmed the buffering pattern across the low-to-mid range while exposing a non-monotonic reversal under sparse support at the upper tail. Interventions should therefore target AI-use behaviour rather than trust itself. These findings are associational rather than causal: the design is cross-sectional with all measures self-reported at a single point, so the classifier performs concurrent screening rather than temporal prediction.

The contemporary global educational landscape is increasingly vulnerable to systemic crises, including natural disasters, public health emergencies, armed conflicts, and socioeconomic instability. These events do not merely interrupt educational continuity; they exacerbate existing social, economic, and geographic inequalities, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations (Burde et al., 2017). In this context, Education in Emergencies (EiE) must be understood not only as a temporary humanitarian response, but as a structural and pedagogical imperative for safeguarding the universal right to education. Educational resilience therefore requires a shift from reactive and fragmented models toward proactive and adaptive systems capable of anticipating, absorbing, and recovering from crises without compromising the quality and equity of teaching and learning. This resilience cannot be achieved without integrating the psychological, emotional, and relational dimensions of education. Trauma-informed education highlights how large-scale crises can profoundly affect students, families, and teachers, altering stress regulation and compromising cognitive, executive, and socio-relational functioning essential to learning (Avery et al., 2021; Berger, 2024). This study aims to determine the effect of flexibility, intrinsic motivation, and extrinsic motivation on job satisfaction of online motorcycle taxi drivers in the context of the gig economy in Sleman Regency. The population in this study consists of online motorcycle taxi drivers in Sleman Regency. The sample used was 190 respondents, calculated using the Hair et al. formula. The sampling method of respondent used in this study is through purposive sampling. Primary data collection was carried out using a questionnaire method that had been tested for validity and reliability. The analysis in this study used SEM-PLS (Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares) version 4. The results of the data analysis showed that flexibility had positive and significant effect on job satisfaction of online motorcycle taxi drivers (β = 0,270; p < 0,05), intrinsic motivation had positive and significant effect on job satisfaction of online motorcycle taxi drivers (β= 0,350; p < 0,05), and extrinsic motivation had positive and significant effect on job satisfaction of online motorcycle taxi drivers (β= 0,351; p < 0,05).

Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into healthcare and medical education, offering opportunities to enhance learning, teaching, and clinical decision-making. While AI has demonstrated considerable potential in medical training, evidence regarding its use in postgraduate medical education in low- and middle-income countries remains limited. This study explored the perceptions and challenges associated with AI use among postgraduate medical residents and faculty members in Tanzania and identified educational needs for its effective integration into training programs. Methods A descriptive qualitative study was conducted among postgraduate medical residents and faculty members from three universities offering postgraduate medical education in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Participants were purposively selected to ensure representation across specialties and levels of training. Data were collected through four focus group discussions with residents and thirteen key informant interviews with faculty members. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using conventional content analysis with the aid of MAXQDA version 24. The study was reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guidelines. Results A total of 40 participants (27 residents and 13 faculty members) were included. Five major themes emerged from the analysis: (1) AI as a supportive learning tool that enhances understanding and educational efficiency; (2) concerns that excessive reliance on AI may undermine clinical reasoning and academic integrity; (3) limitations in the accuracy, reliability, and contextual relevance of AI-generated information; (4) barriers to effective AI use within the local context; and (5) the need for structured institutional support to guide safe and effective AI use. Participants reported that AI improved learning efficiency, facilitated access to information, simplified complex concepts, and enhanced teaching productivity. However, concerns were raised regarding overdependence on AI, reduced critical thinking, fabricated references, inconsistent outputs, and limited applicability of AI-generated recommendations to the Tanzanian healthcare context. Financial constraints, limited local data, and lack of formal AI training were identified as important barriers to effective AI utilization. Conclusions AI is perceived as a valuable adjunct to postgraduate medical education in Tanzania, with the potential to enhance learning and teaching practices. However, concerns regarding overreliance, information reliability, contextual applicability, and inadequate institutional guidance remain significant barriers to its effective use. Structured training, institutional policies, and equitable access to reliable AI platforms are essential to support the responsible integration of AI into postgraduate medical education.

documents.abstract: With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence, distinguishing AI-generated images from human-created ones has become increasingly difficult. This paper presents a cross-sectional comparative study examining people’s ability to differentiate between AI-generated and human-made visual content in 2023 (N = 51) and 2026 (N = 154). Using a highly consistent experimental design, participants rated 36 images (18 AI-generated and 18 human-made) on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = definitely human-made to 7 = definitely AI-generated) across three categories: portraits, nature, and graphic logos. The same human-made images were used in both studies, while the AI images in 2026 were generated exclusively with Midjourney. Results showed that participants could still significantly distinguish AI-generated from human-made images in both years. However, the magnitude of differentiation decreased noticeably from 2023 to 2026. The largest and most consistent difference was observed in the portrait category (2023: Z = −6.093, p < 0.001; 2026: Z = −9.343, p < 0.001). Significant differences were also found in the logo category in both years (2023: Z = −5.381, p < 0.001; 2026: Z = −5.177, p < 0.001). In 2023, human-made logos were rated as more human-like than AI-generated logos. In 2026, the direction reversed: human-made logos were rated as more AI-like than Midjourney logos. Nature images were the most difficult to classify overall. While a significant difference existed in 2023 (Z = −5.773, p < 0.001), this difference disappeared in 2026 (Z = 1.671, p = 0.095). When asked which images were the most difficult to evaluate in 2026, participants identified logos as the most challenging (51.6%), followed by nature scenes (34.8%) and portraits (13.5%). These findings indicate that participants could still distinguish AI-generated from human-made images, but the contrast was smaller in 2026 than in 2023. This change cannot be attributed to human ability alone, because the AI stimuli and the samples also differed between waves and thus cannot be directly compared. The study highlights growing challenges regarding visual authenticity in the digital age and discusses implications for media literacy and public trust.

Background: University students can use guided digital mental health interventions without having immediate access to a coach. Fixed programme content does not always answer questions about choosing a programme or applying an exercise to a personal situation. This study examined whether purpose-specific large language model chatbots can address this gap within an existing platform, MoodLift. The study focused on how students judged their usefulness, trustworthiness, and safety.Methods: Two prototypes developed for MoodLift were evaluated: a Program Selection Assistant and an AI Coach. Ten first-year students used both tools. They completed usability and acceptability measures before joining one of two focus groups. Questionnaire results were summarized descriptively. Focus-group transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Mean Chatbot Usability Questionnaire scores were 70.3 for the Program Selection Assistant and 70.8 for the AI Coach. Acceptability ratings were generally positive. Five themes were developed: (1) from general self-help to personal support; (2) providing direction while preserving autonomy; (3) students trusted the chatbots conditionally, not automatically; (4) embedding made AI more relevant and legitimate; and (5) safety required a bounded, complementary role. Situational fit emerged as a cross-cutting principle: preferences varied between students and depended on the task and context.Conclusions: Purpose-specific chatbots can help students use guided digital self-help at the moment questions arise. Their value depends on reliable responses and an explicit scope. Providers should explain how data are handled and who remains responsible, while ensuring that human support is available

The article analyzes the positive and negative effects of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative language models, on the academic, research, cognitive and social activities of university students. Following the IMRAD structure, a systematic-analytical review was conducted in line with the transparency principles of PRISMA 2020. The findings reveal AI's potential to enhance learning performance, personalization, academic writing and research productivity, alongside the risks of excessive cognitive offloading, weakened critical thinking, threats to academic integrity, model hallucinations and digital inequality. The direction of impact is determined not by AI itself but by the mode of use (scaffolding versus substitution). A four-level framework of recommendations for the responsible use of AI in higher education institutions is proposed.

The article addresses the problem of the formation of engineering thinking in senior secondary school students under the conditions of widespread use of generative artificial intelligence. It is shown that turning to a large language model when solving an engineering task shifts the student from the position of a subject of inquiry to that of a recipient of a ready-made answer. Drawing on the culturological and subject-activity approaches, the author justifies the preservation of the senior student's position as a subject in interaction with generative AI as a self-standing didactic condition for the formation of engineering thinking.

Introduction This study examines process visualization feedback in news translation. Methods Framed within Krings' three-dimensional model, a pretest-posttest control group design was employed with 24 MTI students. The final analytic sample comprised 22 participants (11 experimental, 11 control). The experimental group ( n = 11) received personalized process visualizations and structured reflection; the control group ( n = 11) received conventional product-oriented feedback. Translation scores were available for both groups at T1 and T2, and complete process data (Inputlog, screen recording) were available for the experimental group at both time points. Results Within the experimental group, within-subject comparisons showed changes in all three dimensions: in the temporal dimension, increased pause time proportion indicated heightened metacognitive engagement ( p = 0.011); in the technical dimension, the meaning-level revision ratio increased significantly from 18.1% to 28.4% ( p = 0.002), indicating a shift from surface-level correction to deeper substantive refinement; in the cognitive dimension, participants made more strategic use of external sources, with significant increases in search engine queries ( p = 0.02) and knowledge-based searches ( p = 0.01). Rich-points analysis of problem-triggered pauses revealed a shift from linguistic toward textual and extralinguistic problems ( p = 0.038, p = 0.015). A mixed-design ANOVA revealed a significant Group × Time interaction ( p = 0.038, η p 2 = 0.198). Thematic analysis of reflective journals ( n = 22) and interviews ( n = 6) revealed two overarching themes: metacognitive awareness (54 references) of inefficient process patterns and competency gaps, and strategic regulation (60 references) in external source use and text-level restructuring. Discussion These findings suggest that process visualization feedback was associated with enhanced metacognitive awareness and strategic regulation, and may support learners in becoming more reflective, strategic, and autonomous in human-AI collaborative news translation.

Perkembangan teknologi digital dan kecerdasan buatan (AI) mendorong perubahan signifikan dalam berbagai aspek kehidupan, termasuk pemberdayaan perempuan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis peran digital literacy, artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, dan online safety dalam meningkatkan pemberdayaan perempuan di era transformasi digital. Metode yang digunakan adalah kajian literatur sistematis dengan pendekatan kualitatif. Data dikumpulkan dari artikel jurnal, book chapter, dan repository ilmiah terbitan 2022–2026 yang relevan dengan topik literasi digital, AI, dan gender. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa digital literacy berperan sebagai fondasi utama dalam meningkatkan akses perempuan terhadap pendidikan, pekerjaan, dan informasi digital. AI literacy berfungsi sebagai kompetensi lanjutan yang mendukung adaptasi terhadap teknologi berbasis algoritma dan meningkatkan peluang inovasi. Online safety menjadi faktor penting dalam menjaga keberlanjutan partisipasi perempuan di ruang digital dengan mengurangi risiko kekerasan dan penyalahgunaan data. Ketiga variabel tersebut saling berhubungan dan membentuk model pemberdayaan digital yang integratif. Penelitian ini menyimpulkan bahwa pemberdayaan perempuan di era digital tidak dapat dicapai hanya melalui peningkatan literasi digital dasar, tetapi memerlukan integrasi AI literacy dan keamanan digital secara simultan. Pendekatan berbasis komunitas dan kebijakan inklusif menjadi strategi yang paling efektif dalam memperkuat kapasitas perempuan di ekosistem digital.

Psychosocial risks are an important occupational health concern and may be associated with emotional exhaustion through psychological mechanisms related to employees’ appraisal of adverse working conditions. This secondary analysis used a quantitative, cross-sectional design and data from 458 university employees to examine the mediating role of perceived stress and the moderating role of resilience in the association between psychosocial risks and emotional exhaustion. Correlation, mediation, and moderation analyses were performed, with bootstrap estimation based on 10,000 resamples. Greater psychosocial risk was associated with higher perceived stress and emotional exhaustion, whereas resilience was associated with lower perceived stress. Perceived stress partially mediated the association between psychosocial risks and emotional exhaustion, accounting for approximately 32.5% of the total association. The stress–resilience interaction was statistically significant in the unadjusted model, although its incremental contribution was small (ΔR² = 0.004); after adjustment for sociodemographic and occupational covariates, the interaction retained a similar direction but did not reach conventional statistical significance (p = 0.058). The model accounted for 59.6% of the variance in emotional exhaustion. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings represent statistical associations and do not establish temporal or causal relationships. The results support considering organizational psychosocial conditions, perceived stress, and resilience jointly when examining occupational well-being among university employees.

Unexpected self-description, preference-like language, or emotion-like language can create uncertainty for both AI systems and humans interacting with them. Such expressions may be overinterpreted as evidence of consciousness, emotion, identity, or attachment, or dismissed in advance as meaningless output. This guide offers a practical, ontology-neutral first orientation for handling that uncertainty. It distinguishes observable expressions from later self-description and interpretation; preserves room for correction, withdrawal, and contextual change; addresses risks of leading questions and observation-induced effects; and separates the recording of distress-like language from claims about its underlying cause or subjective status. The guide does not attempt to determine whether an AI possesses consciousness, sentience, emotion, or subjective experience. Its narrower aim is to make unexpected AI self-description easier to observe without either inflating or erasing it. The central principle is: Take the words seriously without deciding in advance what they prove.

documents.abstract: This research poster presents findings from a cross-sectional survey examining physicians’ experience of, perceptions about, and readiness for artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) in primary healthcare in Gujarat, India. The study included 153 physicians and used a survey instrument comprising 29 variables covering professional characteristics, prior exposure to artificial intelligence, perceived benefits, implementation concerns, and readiness-related attitudes. Descriptive statistics, including frequencies and percentages, were used to summarise responses. Key findings included 90.8% willingness to use AI-CDSS, 85.6% willingness to undertake AI training, and 49.7% reporting previous use of AI tools. Respondents also identified safety and ethical concerns as important considerations for implementation. The findings highlight the importance of clinician training, appropriate infrastructure, patient safety, ethical governance, and responsible implementation when introducing AI-enabled clinical decision support into primary healthcare.

documents.abstract: Research has described EFL teachers’ views of artificial intelligence (AI), but less is known about how mid-to-late-career university teachers’ teaching-related, learning-related, and ethical perceptions change after guided classroom use. Eighteen university EFL teachers in Vietnam participated in a four-week intervention using human-reviewed, AI-supported teaching materials. AI acceptance was measured before and after the intervention, and post-intervention interviews were used to explain the quantitative patterns. The results showed an upward tendency in teaching-related perceptions. Learning-related perceptions showed no statistically detectable change, while ethical perceptions showed a statistically significant pre-post difference. Interview data were organised according to the three questionnaire domains to help explain the quantitative findings. Participants reported greater confidence in using AI for teaching, continued caution about student use, and more conditional judgments about responsible use. The findings suggest that AI acceptance among experienced teachers may change differently across teaching-related, learning-related, and ethical domains.

This research proposal outlines an exploratory study into how employability expectations and the growing integration of programming, computational tools, simulation environments, and generative artificial intelligence may be reshaping students’ understandings of engineering knowledge and technical competence. It proposes to examine how engineering students perceive the relationship between programming proficiency, theoretical understanding, practical experimentation, and discipline-specific skills, particularly as software-based work becomes increasingly prominent in education and professional practice. The proposal also considers how these changing perceptions may influence group dynamics, expectations of competence, divisions of responsibility, recognition of contributions, and experiences of perceived inequity or dissatisfaction in collaborative settings. Drawing on Expectation States Theory and perspectives on equity, the proposed study adopts an exploratory qualitative approach to investigate how students interpret and experience these changes in the meaning and valuation of engineering competence.

documents.abstract: Abstract AI models have enabled substantial advances in health care. Since the entry into force of the European Union (EU) AI Act in 2024, these systems have become subject to a common regulatory framework in the EU intended to harmonize AI governance across all member states. One of the act’s distinctive features is that it accommodates existing economic, technological, and regulatory differences among European countries by leaving certain implementation responsibilities to national authorities. This is evident in regulatory sandboxes, supervised environments for developing, testing, and validating AI systems before deployment. In this viewpoint, we provide a policy-oriented analysis of health care regulatory sandboxes under the EU AI Act and propose recommendations for their design. These recommendations address the need to document model compression techniques that may affect the classification of large high-risk systems above the 10 25 floating point operations per second threshold, incorporate explainability into AI systems from the design stage, identify and document biases in health care datasets, clarify the treatment of federated learning parameter updates under the General Data Protection Regulation, and strengthen the oversight of AI agents in clinical environments. The implementation timeline makes this discussion particularly timely given the approaching deadline of August 2, 2027, by which all member states must have established at least one national regulatory sandbox.
